newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK's Tung names his post-1997 cabinet of advisers.
newsitem.headline: HK's Tung names his post-1997 cabinet of advisers.

text.p: Hong Kong's future leader Tung Chee-hwa on Friday named an inner cabinet that included two members who now serve on colonial Governor Chris Patten's council of advisers.

Two members of Patten's Executive Council -- housing authority chief Rosanna Wong and businessman Raymond Ch'ien -- will straddle the handover of Hong Kong to China, which resumes control of the territory at midnight on June 30.

He followed the practice of the departing British administration of reserving slots for Hong Kong's top three civil servants -- currently the Chief Secretary, the Financial Secretary and the Attorney General -- but named no names.

Tung earlier won public acclaim by inviting Hong Kong's popular top civil servant, Chief Secretary Anson Chan, to remain in her post and serve as Administrative Secretary, as the job will be renamed after the handover.
Chan, who serves as Patten's deputy, accepted and is expected to join Tung's Executive Council after the handover.
Tung appointed a veteran adviser to previous colonial governors, Sir S.Y. Chung, to the 15-strong caucus but excluded members of Hong Kong's pro-democracy parties, critics of Beijing.
"There are many capable and dedicated people in the community. Regrettably I cannot include them all in the Executive Council," Tung said in a statement.

Tung, a 59-year-old shipping magnate, was selected last month by a 400-strong China-assembled panel for the post of Chief Executive of post-colonial Hong Kong to step into Patten's shoes when the British depart.
The democrats boycotted the selection process, which they denounced as a travesty of democracy.
"We did not expect him to name anyone from the democratic camp to his inner cabinet," said Democratic Party vice chairman Yeung Sum.
Yeung described the appointees as conservatives. "They fit Mr Tung's style as he is also a conservative himself in his political outlook."
Tung thanked former Executive Councillor Chung, 79, for agreeing to come out of retirement.
His "depth of knowledge about Hong Kong will be of great value to me, especially at this time," the leader-designate said in a statement.

Chung angered Beijing in the early 1980s for expressing a lack of confidence in Hong Kong's future but was later forgiven. His name was one bandied around in the early 1990s as a potential candidate for the job of Chief Executive.
Also in the cabinet was Hong Kong's former Chief Justice, Ti Liang Yang, who relinquished his British knighthood in order to vie with Tung for the Chief Executive's job.
The list came as little surprise in Hong Kong. Most of the members are prominent in the pro-Beijing lobby and sit on China-appointed panels and committees responsible for the handover.
